items.followUp: Classify oxygen, air, brass, water and soil as elements, compounds or mixtures.

rubric.why: Award for correctly identifying tin as an element and Coca-Cola as a mixture.
rubric.description: Tin is an element; Coca-Cola is a mixture.
rubric.how: Check that both classifications are correct.

rubric.why: Award for correctly identifying both as mixtures.
rubric.description: Ice cream and petroleum are mixtures.
rubric.how: Check that both classifications are correct.

rubric.why: Award for correctly identifying gunpowder as a mixture and sugar as a compound.
rubric.description: Gunpowder is a mixture; sugar is a compound.
rubric.how: Check that both classifications are correct.

rubric.why: Award for correctly identifying salt as a compound and blood as a mixture.
rubric.description: Salt is a compound; blood is a mixture.
rubric.how: Check that both classifications are correct.

modelAnswer: (i) Tin — element
(ii) Coca-Cola — mixture
(iii) Ice cream — mixture
(iv) Petroleum — mixture
(v) Gunpowder — mixture
(vi) Sugar — compound
(vii) Salt — compound
(viii) Blood — mixture

items.followUp: Define a covalent compound and state three of its properties.

rubric.why: The definition should describe how ionic compounds form and what holds their ions together.
rubric.description: Definition of an ionic compound.
rubric.how: Award for electron transfer forming oppositely charged ions held by electrostatic attraction.

rubric.why: Ionic compounds have strong attractions between ions, so considerable heat is needed to melt them.
rubric.description: High melting points.
rubric.how: Award for stating that ionic compounds have high melting points.

rubric.why: Ionic compounds conduct when their ions are free to move.
rubric.description: Conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the molten compound or its aqueous solution conducts electricity.

rubric.why: Water commonly separates and surrounds the ions in ionic compounds.
rubric.description: Usually soluble in water.
rubric.how: Award for stating that ionic compounds are generally soluble in water.

modelAnswer: Ionic compounds are formed by the transfer of electrons from one atom to another, producing oppositely charged ions held together by electrostatic attraction.
They usually have high melting and boiling points.
They are usually soluble in water.
They conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water, but not in the solid state.

items.followUp: Explain why a liquid with stronger intermolecular forces generally has a higher boiling point.

rubric.why: Boiling point varies with the kind of liquid and its particles.
rubric.description: Boiling point depends on the nature of the liquid.
rubric.how: Award for noting that different liquids have different boiling points because their nature differs.

rubric.why: Stronger attractions between particles make it harder for them to escape into the gas state.
rubric.description: Stronger intermolecular forces give a higher boiling point.
rubric.how: Award for correctly linking stronger intermolecular forces with a higher boiling point.

rubric.why: Weaker attractions are overcome more easily, so less heating is needed to boil the liquid.
rubric.description: Weaker intermolecular forces give a lower boiling point.
rubric.how: Award for correctly linking weaker intermolecular forces with a lower boiling point.

rubric.why: The explanation should connect boiling with the energy needed to overcome attractions between particles.
rubric.description: More heat is needed to overcome stronger forces and separate particles.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that heat is required to overcome intermolecular forces as the liquid boils.

modelAnswer: The boiling point depends on the nature of the liquid and the strength of the forces between its particles.
A liquid with stronger intermolecular forces has a higher boiling point because more heat is needed to overcome those forces and separate the particles.
A liquid with weaker intermolecular forces has a lower boiling point because less heat is needed to separate its particles.

items.followUp: Give two differences between a pure compound and a mixture.

rubric.why: A substance has a definite composition, unlike a mixture whose composition can vary.
rubric.description: Difference in composition.
rubric.how: Award for stating that a substance has fixed composition while a mixture can have variable composition.

rubric.why: Mixture components can be separated physically; the components of a compound require chemical separation.
rubric.description: Difference in separation and component properties.
rubric.how: Award for stating that mixtures are separated by physical methods, unlike compounds which require chemical methods.

modelAnswer: A substance is pure and has a fixed composition and definite properties; a mixture has variable composition.
The components of a mixture retain their properties and can be separated by physical methods; the components of a compound are chemically combined and require chemical methods for separation.

items.followUp: Calculate the number of moles in 24 g of magnesium. Use a molar mass of 24 g mol⁻¹.

rubric.why: The mole calculation uses mass divided by molar mass.
rubric.description: Correct formula for amount of substance.
rubric.how: Award for writing or clearly using n = m/M.

rubric.why: The calculated amount is three quarters of a mole.
rubric.description: Correct numerical answer with unit.
rubric.how: Award for 0.75 mol or an equivalent value with the mole unit.

modelAnswer: Given: mass of carbon, m = 9.0 g = 0.0090 kg; molar mass of carbon, M = 12 g mol⁻¹ = 0.012 kg mol⁻¹.
Formula: n = m / M.
Substitution: n = 0.0090 kg / 0.012 kg mol⁻¹.
Answer: n = 0.75 mol.

items.followUp: State one limitation of Rutherford’s atomic model concerning the stability of atoms.

rubric.why: The model could not explain why orbiting electrons do not lose energy and collapse into the nucleus.
rubric.description: Failure to explain atomic stability.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that the model predicted electrons would lose energy and fall into the nucleus, making atoms unstable.

rubric.why: The model did not explain the discrete line spectra of atoms.
rubric.description: Failure to explain atomic line spectra.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the model could not explain the line spectrum or arrangement of electrons in atoms.

modelAnswer: Rutherford’s model could not explain the stability of the atom: orbiting electrons should radiate energy and fall into the nucleus.
It could not explain the discrete line spectra of atoms or the arrangement of electrons around the nucleus.

items.followUp: Name one radioactive isotope used to treat cancer and state its use.

rubric.why: A valid isotope used in radiotherapy must be named.
rubric.description: First isotope used in radiotherapy.
rubric.how: Award for naming a recognised radiotherapy isotope, such as cobalt-60.

rubric.why: A second valid isotope used in radiotherapy must be named.
rubric.description: Second isotope used in radiotherapy.
rubric.how: Award for naming another recognised therapeutic radioisotope, such as iodine-131 for thyroid treatment.

modelAnswer: Cobalt-60 is used in radiotherapy to treat cancer.
Iodine-131 is also used for treatment of thyroid disorders, including thyroid cancer.

items.followUp: State how the long form periodic table is arranged and give its number of groups.

rubric.why: The modern long-form table orders elements by atomic number.
rubric.description: Arrangement of elements.
rubric.how: Award for stating that elements are arranged in increasing atomic number.

rubric.why: The long-form periodic table has eighteen vertical groups.
rubric.description: Number of groups.
rubric.how: Award for stating that it has 18 groups.

modelAnswer: In the long-form periodic table, elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number.
It has 18 vertical groups and 7 horizontal periods.
